> > > >
> > > >  What are the differences between the original LDSC and the multivariate LDSC in Genomic SEM, and how are the new additions used later? It would be great if someone could give us a clarification in addition to how the method is described in the paper. Are there other differences apart from the estimation of the sampling covariances?
> > > Apart from some minor differences in QC defaults, the only substantive difference is that multivariate LDSC produces the off-diagonals of V, i.e. the sampling covariances of the estimates, (and also conveniently produces S as a full matrix rather than as a sequence of pairwise rGs). Note that multivariate ldsc function can now produce S and V in standardized forms (i.e. an rG matrix and its associated sampling covariance matrix) using  the argument 'stand'. You can of course verify that results are nearly equivalent by running the same set of sumstats through both programs and comparing the point estimates for h2, rg, and their SEs. We have done this rather extensively.
> > > >
> > > > For performing latent factor GWAS with Genomic SEM, would it be possible to include automatic checks and warnings when the original dataset effect standard errors are outside of what is expected from their supposed scale? Would it be possible to add the functionality to automatically convert the standard errors between scales?
> > > We have automated some detection of whether effect sizes are betas or ORs, but it is difficult to know whether the betas are logistic, OLS, or linear probability model, and whether the SEs are provided for betas or ORs without well-documented sumstats from their original sources. If p, SE, and effect size are provided, you can determine whether the effect size is indeed a regression beta or an OR by examining whether the values are distributed closer to 1 (null for OR) or 0 (null for beta). You can then determine whether the SE is for the beta or OR by examining whether you recapture the reported p value using the beta/SE (or [OR-1]/SE ) ratio with or without converting the SE via the formula we provide in our paper (logistic SE = odds ratio SE/OR). This is something that we may be able to further automate down the road.
> > >
> > > Note that we already do convert estimates to and STDY scale (i.e. expected sd difference in Y per 1 unit shift in the effect allele), and we provide capability to convert linear probability model coefficients and their SEs to logistic coefficients and SEs.
> > > >
> > > > There are, or were at least, some R-packages that were able to create path diagrams using lavaan results. Would it be possible to make lavaan results corresponding to the Genomic SEM results available as part of the usermodel output?
> > > We have discussed this and it is something that is of potential interest to us, but may be rather involved on the programming side. I am personally of the opinion that forcing a user to translate input and output manually to a path diagram that they draw themselves helps to ensure that users have developed a higher level of the understanding of the models they are fitting. I also find automatically generated path diagrams to be suboptimal for publications.
> > > >
> > > > How would you interpret a latent factor Genomic SEM model where the latent factors are uncorrelated? Would it be viable in any situation to set latent factors as uncorrelated, and how would it be useful?
> > > That's a difficult question to provide a blanket answer to, as it depends on the features of model as a whole. If fitting a cholesky decomposition, or a GWAS-by-subtraction (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.01.14.905794v1), then it is important to specify that latent factors are uncorrelated, so as to properly interpret the downstream latent variables as independent components of vairance, or residuals. If fitting a hierarchical model or bifactor model, the correlations among the indicators is subsumed by the general factor, and the domai-specific factors (or their residuals) should therefore be specified as orthogonal to ensure proper interpretation and model identification. If fitting a correlated factors model with simple structure (i.e. no cross-loadings), then I think it may be overly restrictive to fix the correlations between the factors to 0 by assumption rather than freely estimate them. Generally, this is the sort of question that is more generally relevant to SEM, not just Genomic SEM, so I would advise consulting a textbook, such as Kline (Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling) or Loehlin (Latent Variable Models).

> > > > Best,

messages.subject_clean: Regarding GWAS by subtraction Model equations.
messages.body_plain:
Dear Veera,

These are all good questions.

First, absent coding typos (such as the missing + that you previously caught), the model from slide 37 from the talk I previously linked to and the model in the GWAS-by-Subtraction tutorial are equivalent. The "slide 37 model" implements GWAS-by-subtraction via regression whereas the "tutorial model" implements it via Cholesky decomposition. You can read more about Cholesky models in SEM contexts in this paper by Loehlin: https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02361160. The difference between the two implementations is that the "slide 37 model" keeps the two components (e.g. the "Cog" and "NonCog" components) in their original units, such that the total genetic variance of each component is its SNP heritability, whereas the "tutorial model" places the two components in Z-units, such that the total genetic variance of each component is equal to 1.0 (the units are not thrown out, as the information is now captured in the loadings on the Cholesky factors). The genetic correlations between sumstats formed from the two approaches will equal 1.0, and both approaches will produce equivalent genetic correlations (i.e. standardized covariances) with collateral phenotypes. Additionally, if you were to plot the SNP betas (e.g. for a subset of SNPs for ease) from the two approaches, you would also find that they are on different units but are perfectly correlated.

Second, you are correct regarding the use of NA and start(). NA freely estimates a parameter (lavaan's default is to fix the first loading to 1.0). start() provides a starting value other than the lavaan default (I believe that this often is a 1 or a 0 depending on the parameter). Numerical optimization is iterative, which means that the model is fit first using the starting values, then adjusts the values in increments or decrements and determines whether the adjustment has increased or reduced model fit, and does this over and over again until some convergence criterion is achieved indicating the the maximum fit has been achieved. There are various reasons for providing your own starting values. Some are: a) speeding up run-time (so fewer iterations are needed for a model to converge), b) facilitating model convergence (e.g., when the model "times out" and fails to converge using the default start values), c) preventing the model from converging on local fit maxima that depart from the global maximum, d) preventing the model from converging on an equivalent, but less interpretable, solution to the preferred solution (e.g. in some models with latent variables, such as the Cholesky, when all regression paths are negative, the solution is equivalent to the preferred solution with them all being positive; the negative solution provides the same interpretation, but the factors must be conceptualized as being "reverse coded," e.g. higher scores corresponding with lower education, which can be confusing). Useful start values are informed guesses about the likely parameter value, such as the estimate from a previous run of a simpler model (e.g. the model without the SNP). Or for example, a value above zero and less than 1.0 for the genetic variance of a GWAS phenotype (because we know that its SNP heritability is greater than 0 and far less than 1.0) Overriding the defaults if often unnecessary, but can be helpful for the reasons I outline here.

I think that some of these clarifications are worth putting into our tutorial. We'll put it on our to do list. In the meantime, feel free to reach out with further questions.

All the best,

Elliot

P.S. If you are looking for a very brief introduction to SEM, I suggest McArdle & Boker's Path Analysis and Path Diagrams chapter (https://doi.org/10.1002/0470013192.bsa471). Accessible books are Loehlin's Latent Variable Models and Kline's Principals and Practices of Structural Equation Modeling, both of which I use in my graduate SEM course. A much more advanced book is Bollen's Structural Equations with Latent Variables.

--

Hi Andrew, Eliot, and Michel,

Hope this finds you doing well and enjoying your summer (at least as best you can, given the current circumstances). I had 2 quick questions for you. We have been conducting a multivariate GWAS on the four higher-order Psychopathology factors that we found in our structural analyses described in our forthcoming World Psychiatry paper (see biorxiv #https://doi.org/10.1101/502039). One of the things we’d like to report along with the other analyses is the percent of the genetic correlations among the four Psychopathology factors accounted for by all of the SNPs. Can we get this by using the genetic correlations that could be reported in the measurement model output for the mvgwas and comparing those to the genetic correlations that are reported in the output for the measurement model alone, that is without doing the mvgwas? And is it possible to get such output for the measurement model in the overall mvgwas, rather than the measurement model for each SNP?  Second, in conducting post-GWAS analyses of each factor (e.g., gene-based tests) we need to specify the N for the GWAS for each factor. Would it be more appropriate to use the overall N for the mvgwas, given that the 4 factors are correlated, or the overall summed N for the constituent GWASs for each factor?

Thanks!
Irwin

Hi Irwin,

Please see my thoughts below.

All the best,

Elliot

> One of the things we’d like to report along with the other analyses is the percent of the genetic correlations among the four Psychopathology factors accounted for by all of the SNPs.

I'm not sure what you mean here. The LDSC estimates of genetic covariance among phenotyeps (or the genetic correlations among latent factors estimated from a no-SNP model) are indeed the genetic correlations accounted for by all of the SNPs. If you are interested in the extent to which the model produces expectations that are consistent with the unmodelled LDSC strucuture, you can you standar LISREL matrix algebra, or path tracing rules, to produce the expected covariances and plot them against the LDSC-estiamted covariances. We do an example of this in the Appendix of the de la Fuente paper ( <http://goog_191200428>https://doi.org/10.1101/766600).

If alternatively you are interested in the residual covariance between factors after accounting for a linear combination of the (noisy) betas from all SNPs, you'd need to do something like residualize the genetic covariance matrix for the expectation of a polygenic score derived from the sumstats from your multivariate model. I haven't worked that math out, but I would recommend against it for the very same reason that you don't want test what proportion of SNP h2 is accounted for by a PGS effect estimated in the same data in which the sumstats to produce the PGS were derived.

> Can we get this by using the genetic correlations that could be reported in the measurement model output for the mvgwas and comparing those to the genetic correlations that are reported in the output for the measurement model alone, that is without doing the mvgwas?

> First, absent coding typos (such as the missing + that you previously caught), the model from slide 37 from the talk I previously linked to and the model in the GWAS-by-Subtraction tutorial are equivalent. The "slide 37 model" implements GWAS-by-subtraction via regression whereas the "tutorial model" implements it via Cholesky decomposition. You can read more about Cholesky models in SEM contexts in this paper by Loehlin: https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02361160. The difference between the two implementations is that the "slide 37 model" keeps the two components (e.g. the "Cog" and "NonCog" components) in their original units, such that the total genetic variance of each component is its SNP heritability, whereas the "tutorial model" places the two components in Z-units, such that the total genetic variance of each component is equal to 1.0 (the units are not thrown out, as the information is now captured in the loadings on the Cholesky factors). The genetic correlations between sumstats formed from the two approaches will equal 1.0, and both approaches will produce equivalent genetic correlations (i.e. standardized covariances) with collateral phenotypes. Additionally, if you were to plot the SNP betas (e.g. for a subset of SNPs for ease) from the two approaches, you would also find that they are on different units but are perfectly correlated.
>
> Second, you are correct regarding the use of NA and start(). NA freely estimates a parameter (lavaan's default is to fix the first loading to 1.0). start() provides a starting value other than the lavaan default (I believe that this often is a 1 or a 0 depending on the parameter). Numerical optimization is iterative, which means that the model is fit first using the starting values, then adjusts the values in increments or decrements and determines whether the adjustment has increased or reduced model fit, and does this over and over again until some convergence criterion is achieved indicating the the maximum fit has been achieved. There are various reasons for providing your own starting values. Some are: a) speeding up run-time (so fewer iterations are needed for a model to converge), b) facilitating model convergence (e.g., when the model "times out" and fails to converge using the default start values), c) preventing the model from converging on local fit maxima that depart from the global maximum, d) preventing the model from converging on an equivalent, but less interpretable, solution to the preferred solution (e.g. in some models with latent variables, such as the Cholesky, when all regression paths are negative, the solution is equivalent to the preferred solution with them all being positive; the negative solution provides the same interpretation, but the factors must be conceptualized as being "reverse coded," e.g. higher scores corresponding with lower education, which can be confusing). Useful start values are informed guesses about the likely parameter value, such as the estimate from a previous run of a simpler model (e.g. the model without the SNP). Or for example, a value above zero and less than 1.0 for the genetic variance of a GWAS phenotype (because we know that its SNP heritability is greater than 0 and far less than 1.0) Overriding the defaults if often unnecessary, but can be helpful for the reasons I outline here.

Ah, I seen your detailed post contained awnsers to  most of my questions ;)

1. I don't think in any one situation one model it better then the other, in fact one of the two "residual" models is exactly the same as the cholesky:

model_res <- "model1 <- 'CP  ~ B*SNP
            EA ~ CP + A*SNP"

can be transformed to:

model<-'C=~NA*EA +start(0.2)*EA + start(0.5)*CP
         NC=~NA*EA +start(0.2)*EA

         C~B*SNP
         NC~ A*SNP

         NC~~1*NC
         C~~1*C
         C~~0*NC

         CP ~~ 0*EA
         CP~~0*CP
         EA~~0*EA
         SNP~~SNP'

Where B should be B and A should be A.

the GWIS model was mainly developed as some point to show in Grotzinger et al that genomicSEM is a versatile tool that can also perfrom "GWIS".

The GWIS models are themselfs in turn transformations of each-other I believe (harder to figure out). Currently I would recommend people use the Cholesky, I feel its a more natural representation (both parameters estimated in 1 model), and it has a lot of empirical work (see our paper) as suport for the validity of Cog and NonCog (where NonCog is the non-cognitive contribution to education specifically.). But the bottom line is all 3 models are representations of the same underlying data. The key of the difference you are detecting ids that you are comparing 2 models (the two GWAIS, which are mutually dependent, also see the original GWIS paper for details on that) with 1 model.

I would still like to see the exact models you are fitting to be certain we are on one page. If you email us and are willing to share the goal of your study  we could help you pick the best parameterisation for the exact questions you are trying to awnser (but I understand if you want to keep that private).

Best,
Michel

But the bottom line is all 3 models are representations of the same underlying data.

If you want to share the goal of your study (either here or privately in an email to me and Elliot) we can help you pick the best parameterization.

Best,

Michel

You can read more about Cholesky models in SEM contexts in this paper by Loehlin: https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02361160. Numerical optimization is iterative, which means that the model is fit first using the starting values, then adjusts the values in increments or decrements and determines whether the adjustment has increased or reduced model fit, and does this over and over again until some convergence criterion is achieved indicating the the maximum fit has been achieved. > > > > >
> > > > >  What are the differences between the original LDSC and the multivariate LDSC in Genomic SEM, and how are the new additions used later? It would be great if someone could give us a clarification in addition to how the method is described in the paper. Are there other differences apart from the estimation of the sampling covariances?
> > > > Apart from some minor differences in QC defaults, the only substantive difference is that multivariate LDSC produces the off-diagonals of V, i.e. the sampling covariances of the estimates, (and also conveniently produces S as a full matrix rather than as a sequence of pairwise rGs). Note that multivariate ldsc function can now produce S and V in standardized forms (i.e. an rG matrix and its associated sampling covariance matrix) using  the argument 'stand'. You can of course verify that results are nearly equivalent by running the same set of sumstats through both programs and comparing the point estimates for h2, rg, and their SEs. We have done this rather extensively.
> > > > >
> > > > > For performing latent factor GWAS with Genomic SEM, would it be possible to include automatic checks and warnings when the original dataset effect standard errors are outside of what is expected from their supposed scale? Would it be possible to add the functionality to automatically convert the standard errors between scales?
> > > > We have automated some detection of whether effect sizes are betas or ORs, but it is difficult to know whether the betas are logistic, OLS, or linear probability model, and whether the SEs are provided for betas or ORs without well-documented sumstats from their original sources. If p, SE, and effect size are provided, you can determine whether the effect size is indeed a regression beta or an OR by examining whether the values are distributed closer to 1 (null for OR) or 0 (null for beta). You can then determine whether the SE is for the beta or OR by examining whether you recapture the reported p value using the beta/SE (or [OR-1]/SE ) ratio with or without converting the SE via the formula we provide in our paper (logistic SE = odds ratio SE/OR). This is something that we may be able to further automate down the road.
> > > >
> > > > Note that we already do convert estimates to and STDY scale (i.e. expected sd difference in Y per 1 unit shift in the effect allele), and we provide capability to convert linear probability model coefficients and their SEs to logistic coefficients and SEs.
> > > > >
> > > > > There are, or were at least, some R-packages that were able to create path diagrams using lavaan results. Would it be possible to make lavaan results corresponding to the Genomic SEM results available as part of the usermodel output?
> > > > We have discussed this and it is something that is of potential interest to us, but may be rather involved on the programming side. I am personally of the opinion that forcing a user to translate input and output manually to a path diagram that they draw themselves helps to ensure that users have developed a higher level of the understanding of the models they are fitting. I also find automatically generated path diagrams to be suboptimal for publications.
> > > > >
> > > > > How would you interpret a latent factor Genomic SEM model where the latent factors are uncorrelated? Would it be viable in any situation to set latent factors as uncorrelated, and how would it be useful?
> > > > That's a difficult question to provide a blanket answer to, as it depends on the features of model as a whole. If fitting a cholesky decomposition, or a GWAS-by-subtraction (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.01.14.905794v1), then it is important to specify that latent factors are uncorrelated, so as to properly interpret the downstream latent variables as independent components of vairance, or residuals. If fitting a hierarchical model or bifactor model, the correlations among the indicators is subsumed by the general factor, and the domai-specific factors (or their residuals) should therefore be specified as orthogonal to ensure proper interpretation and model identification. If fitting a correlated factors model with simple structure (i.e. no cross-loadings), then I think it may be overly restrictive to fix the correlations between the factors to 0 by assumption rather than freely estimate them. Generally, this is the sort of question that is more generally relevant to SEM, not just Genomic SEM, so I would advise consulting a textbook, such as Kline (Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling) or Loehlin (Latent Variable Models).

Hi Michel and Elliot
thanks for getting back quickly.

I've incorporated the workflow in a snakemake pipeline. So it'll not make sense to share the exact code. I've summarised the workflow process below (Sorry, If I have mistyped some parts of it, as I am manually typing it below). But you let me know if any of the steps here are not clear.

First I munge the files individually.

munge(files="CP.sumstats", N=NA,  info.filter=0.9, maf.filter=0.01, hm3="w_hm3.noMHC.snplist", trait.names="CP")
munge(files="EA3.sumstats", N=NA, info.filter=0.9, maf.filter=0.01, hm3="w_hm3.noMHC.snplist", trait.names="EA3")

N= NA, because I included N column in the sumstats file itself. (N as per the readme files in SSGAC website EA3=766345; CP=257828)

Next, I created the ldsc output using the following command.

ldscoutput = ldsc(traits=c("CP.sumstats.munged.sumstats.gz","EA3.sumstats.munged.sumstats.gz"), sample.prev=c(NA,NA), population.prev=c(NA,NA), ld="eur_w_ld_chr", wld="eur_w_ld_chr", trait.names=c("CP","EA3"), ldsc.log="out.log"))

Next, I created the sumstats file.

p_sumstats = sumstats(files=c("CP.sumstats","EA3.sumstats"), ref="reference.1000G.maf.0.005.txt", trait.names=c("CP","EA3"), se.logit=c(T,T), OLS=NULL, linprob=NULL, prop=NULL, N=NULL, info.filter=0.90,maf.filter=0.01)

Then, I defined the gwis models.
gwis.model1 = 'CP ~ SNP
EA3 ~ CP + SNP'
gwis.model2 = 'EA3 ~ SNP
CP ~ EA3 + SNP'

Then I ran the GWAS for two models.

gwas1 = userGWAS(covstruc = ldscoutput, SNPs = p_sumstats, estimation = "DWLS", model=gwis.model1, sub = c('CP~SNP', 'EA3~SNP'), parallel=FALSE)
gwas2 = userGWAS(covstruc = ldscoutput, SNPs = p_sumstats, estimation = "DWLS", model=gwis.model2, sub = c('CP~SNP', 'EA3~SNP'), parallel=FALSE)

In the GWAS output, I get two effect sizes: one for CP and other for EA3. In the gwas1, I discarded the CP effect sizes as it's almost the same as the original CP GWAS. In the gwas2, I discarded the EA3 effect sizes as they are almost the same as the original EA3 GWAS.

I parallelized the process by splitting the p_sumstats into chunks and running GWAS of each chunk separately in parallel. Then I concatenated the GWAS output. In the SEM sumstats, I used the same N as the original GWASs (noncog=766345; cog=257828)

Please let me know in which step I made a mistake.

Thanks.

You can read more about Cholesky models in SEM contexts in this paper by Loehlin: https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02361160. The genetic correlations between sumstats formed from the two approaches will equal 1.0, and both approaches will produce equivalent genetic correlations (i.e. standardized covariances) with collateral phenotypes. NA freely estimates a parameter (lavaan's default is to fix the first loading to 1.0). start() provides a starting value other than the lavaan default (I believe that this often is a 1 or a 0 depending on the parameter). Numerical optimization is iterative, which means that the model is fit first using the starting values, then adjusts the values in increments or decrements and determines whether the adjustment has increased or reduced model fit, and does this over and over again until some convergence criterion is achieved indicating the the maximum fit has been achieved. Dear Veera,
OK, so I think I see at least part of where we are missing each other. You are estimating an EA-minus-Cog factor (i.e. a "NonCog" factor) in one model and a Cog-minus-EA factor (i.e a "non-EA" factor) in another model. Each of your two models outputs two sets of sumstats but you are discarding one set from each. This isn't what we are doing. In Demange et al., we fit a model that decomposes EA genetics into Cog genetics and NonCog genetics. We don't fit a model that decomposes Cog genetics into EA genetics and Non-EA genetics. You must be correlating your "Non-EA" factor (what you call Cog-residual) with our Cognitive factor (which is just the original cognitive performance GWAS). If you want to validate that the regression based (slide 37) parameterization against the output from the Demange et al. Cholesky parameterization, you will only need to run the first of your two models to produce the Cog and NonCog sumstats. The Cog sumstats that you discard are indeed equivalent, apart from rescaling, to the Cog sumstats from Demange et al. The EA-minus-Cog sumstats that you retain are equivalent, apart from rescaling, to the NonCog sumstats from Demange et al. If you want to run the other model to residualize Cog from EA, you certainly can, but we have not done that so there is nothing from Demange et al. to compare your results to.
As per your last email, let's plan to continue the conversation regarding your specific application by email. We will post to the group if more general points of clarification come up.
All the best,
Elliot

> > > > > > First, absent coding typos (such as the missing + that you previously caught), the model from slide 37 from the talk I previously linked to and the model in the GWAS-by-Subtraction tutorial are equivalent. The "slide 37 model" implements GWAS-by-subtraction via regression whereas the "tutorial model" implements it via Cholesky decomposition. You can read more about Cholesky models in SEM contexts in this paper by Loehlin: https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02361160. The difference between the two implementations is that the "slide 37 model" keeps the two components (e.g. the "Cog" and "NonCog" components) in their original units, such that the total genetic variance of each component is its SNP heritability, whereas the "tutorial model" places the two components in Z-units, such that the total genetic variance of each component is equal to 1.0 (the units are not thrown out, as the information is now captured in the loadings on the Cholesky factors). The genetic correlations between sumstats formed from the two approaches will equal 1.0, and both approaches will produce equivalent genetic correlations (i.e. standardized covariances) with collateral phenotypes. Additionally, if you were to plot the SNP betas (e.g. for a subset of SNPs for ease) from the two approaches, you would also find that they are on different units but are perfectly correlated.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Second, you are correct regarding the use of NA and start(). NA freely estimates a parameter (lavaan's default is to fix the first loading to 1.0). start() provides a starting value other than the lavaan default (I believe that this often is a 1 or a 0 depending on the parameter). Numerical optimization is iterative, which means that the model is fit first using the starting values, then adjusts the values in increments or decrements and determines whether the adjustment has increased or reduced model fit, and does this over and over again until some convergence criterion is achieved indicating the the maximum fit has been achieved. There are various reasons for providing your own starting values. Some are: a) speeding up run-time (so fewer iterations are needed for a model to converge), b) facilitating model convergence (e.g., when the model "times out" and fails to converge using the default start values), c) preventing the model from converging on local fit maxima that depart from the global maximum, d) preventing the model from converging on an equivalent, but less interpretable, solution to the preferred solution (e.g. in some models with latent variables, such as the Cholesky, when all regression paths are negative, the solution is equivalent to the preferred solution with them all being positive; the negative solution provides the same interpretation, but the factors must be conceptualized as being "reverse coded," e.g. higher scores corresponding with lower education, which can be confusing). Useful start values are informed guesses about the likely parameter value, such as the estimate from a previous run of a simpler model (e.g. the model without the SNP). Or for example, a value above zero and less than 1.0 for the genetic variance of a GWAS phenotype (because we know that its SNP heritability is greater than 0 and far less than 1.0) Overriding the defaults if often unnecessary, but can be helpful for the reasons I outline here.

This is a great question that I can hopefully provide some clarity on and help troubleshoot. To start, run time is going to depend on three main factors:
1. The number of SNPs left after running the sumstats function. Here, I wonder if you are left with quite a few more variants relative to the example on the github.

2. How fast the model without individual SNPs runs (and relatedly, how well it fits the data). I know for me the Tourette Syndrome summary statistics have generally caused problems with model convergence depending on the included traits. A good test here would be to run the commonfactor function using just the ldsc output and see what the data looks like. It might take only .5 seconds longer than the example on the github, but that scales up pretty quickly with respect to total run time when the model is being estimated across a million plus SNPs.

3. The computing power for whatever you are using to run your analyses. For most computing clusters, my sense is a standard number of cores for a single run is 12+ (on our computing cluster it's 24 cores per run). With that said, I would recommend using more than the 4 cores initially used if possible.

To summarize, I would recommend taking a look at how well a common factor model fits the data, determine how many SNPs are being analyzed based on the number of rows in the sumstats output, and increase the number of cores if possible. If the end result is you have a model that fits the data well, but have a lot of SNPs or the model takes a little longer to estimate, I would additionally recommend splitting up the data across different jobs. I know others have written scripts that will automatically split the sumstats output into chunks of 20 or so and automatically send off 20 different jobs. As the model estimated for each SNP is entirely independent of one another, how the data is split is completely up to you. As a final troubleshooting option, you might try running a subset of 5,000 SNPs just to make sure it isn't a more general bug. Let me know if you have any other questions!

Best,
  Andrew

So model fits the data well (briefly: the chisq test, which tests the model against a freely estimated covariance matrix isnt significant, which means the model doest describe the covariance significantly worse, CFI is 1, CFI ranges form 0 to 1 and is a comparison against an "empty" model where the traits are uncorrelated, 1 means good ft compared to an empty model. then the SRMR quantifies the (weighted I believe) squared difference between the observed and expected covariance matrix, its lowish here, which is good.

This all being said, the model fits the covariance matrix well, but the factor doest explain a lot of the heritable variation in for example TS ( .114^2 / (.114^2 + .199) = ~6%)

so if you added TS because you are interested in genetic effects on TS be forewarned this factor isn't really a reflection of TS (because TS doest correlate to highly with the other traits I think)

Your model is slower than usual I'd sya, but not entirely unheard off. To speed things up you can specify starting values near (but not at!) the final estimates and perhaps things go a bit quicker.

Best,
Michel
